threads.thread_goal: Align on current-state workflows and confirm scope for standardisation

messages.text: Kicking off the intake workflow project for project_title: Rollout of Standardised Patient Intake and Admin Workflow. For this first thread, can we map how patient intake and basic admin tasks currently run in each unit so we can progress T1 and start shaping A1. Please share for your unit: 1) which intake scenarios you see most often (eg adult, older adult, disability support, walk-ins vs scheduled), 2) a simple step list from first contact to handover to clinical staff, 3) any variations between shifts or days. Also, we need to agree which units and scenarios are in scope for the first standardisation wave and how detailed the workflow maps should be. I suggest we focus on three representative units and capture enough detail to see handoffs, documents used, and common pain points.

For my unit, the main scenarios are older adults with scheduled appointments and some disability support cases. Rough current flow: 1) patient arrives and gives name and appointment time, 2) we check the schedule and confirm ID with card or document, 3) we ask them to fill in the intake and consent forms we use now, 4) we check that all required fields are filled, especially consent and GP details, 5) we hand the file to the nurse or healthcare assistant and update the board. Variations: on busy mornings, sometimes consent is double checked by the nurse instead of admin. Pain points: forms are slightly different between morning and evening shifts, and some staff still use older templates. This should definitely be in scope for the first wave.

In my previous unit, we had mostly adult and older adult scheduled visits, plus a few walk-ins. Steps were: 1) greet patient and confirm appointment, 2) check ID and health card, 3) give them the intake form and a separate consent form, 4) once returned, we quickly scan for missing fields, 5) we enter basic data into the system and put the paper file in the tray for the nurse. On late shifts, sometimes we skip the quick scan because of time pressure and the nurse finds missing consent later. That causes delays and extra trips back to reception. I think this unit type is also important for the first standardisation wave.

From what I see in our disability support clinic: 1) patient or carer arrives, 2) we check their name and if they have an appointment, 3) we give them the same intake form as the general clinic, 4) sometimes we add an extra sheet for disability details, 5) we pass everything to the nurse. I am not sure if this counts as a separate scenario or if we treat it like the others. Also, I do not know how much detail you need in the map, should I include things like when we call the nurse to say the patient is here.

That disability support flow is useful. I would treat it as a distinct intake scenario because of the extra sheet and the involvement of carers. For the level of detail in A1 and T1, I suggest we include: 1) each step where the patient or carer interacts with admin or clinical staff, 2) each document or form used, including that extra disability sheet, 3) each handoff point, like when you call the nurse or move the file. We do not need every micro action, but we should capture where errors or delays tend to appear, such as missing consent or incomplete disability information.

Agree that we should show the handoffs and the documents. I can help list where we usually see issues with consent and identification, especially when carers sign. For my last shift in the general clinic, the main variation was that on weekends we sometimes skip the verbal explanation of the consent form because it is busy. That might be important to capture in the map so we can fix it later.

On the question about scope: based on what you all shared, I propose that for the first standardisation wave we include three scenarios: 1) scheduled adult and older adult visits in the general clinic, 2) disability support clinic visits where a carer may be involved, 3) walk-ins that are handled through the same reception. Units in scope would then be the main general clinic, the older adult focused unit, and the disability support clinic. Emergency intake and inpatient admissions would stay out of scope for now. If no one objects by tomorrow, I will record this as our agreed scope.

Scope proposal works for me. Leaving emergency and inpatient out for now makes sense because their intake is very different and more time critical. For the maps, I can draft the flow for the older adult unit with the steps you listed and highlight where we sometimes skip checks when it is busy.

The suggested detail level is clear. I will map the general clinic scheduled visits and walk-ins. I will include: greeting, ID check, forms given, quick review, data entry, and handover to nurse or healthcare assistant. I will also note where we see missing consent or incomplete contact details. Once I have a draft, I will ask one nurse and one healthcare assistant to validate it so we meet the validation part of T1.

No objections from me on the scope. I will focus on the disability support clinic scenario and try to describe the steps with the carer involvement. I might need someone to double check that I capture the handoff to the nurse correctly, because sometimes the nurse comes to reception and sometimes we just send the file.

Happy to review the disability support map with you. We should make sure we show both options: nurse coming to reception and file transfer only. That will help later when we standardise the handoff in A1 and then in the SOP.

When you map the general clinic, can you also note if we explain the consent form verbally or just hand it over. From the compliance side, that difference might matter later when we align with the quality and compliance officer.

Good point, I will add a step for verbal explanation of consent and mark where it is sometimes skipped on late shifts. That should make it visible in A1 so we can address it when we design the standard process.

To close this out: we have alignment that the first wave covers the main general clinic, the older adult unit, and the disability support clinic, focusing on scheduled adult and older adult visits plus walk-ins, including disability support with carers. We also agreed that workflow maps for A1 under T1 will show: patient and carer interactions, documents and forms used, and handoffs between admin and clinical staff, with pain points and variations noted. I will document this as our baseline and move us to drafting the maps.

threads.thread_goal: Review and finalise the draft standard intake SOP and forms

messages.text: I have uploaded the first draft of the Standard Patient Intake SOP and the unified intake and consent form templates for project_title: Rollout of Standardised Patient Intake and Admin Workflow. These correspond to A2 and A3 and are based on the workflow maps in A1 and the work under T2 and T3. Please review with three questions in mind: 1) Are the core steps and responsibilities clear and realistic for your unit, 2) Do the forms capture all information you usually need without adding unnecessary fields, 3) Any compliance or consent concerns we should flag before sending to the quality and compliance officer. Share comments in this thread so we can converge on final versions for the pilot.

I went through A2. The overall flow matches what we do, but I have two suggestions: 1) In the identification step, can we explicitly state that ID must be checked against both the appointment list and the health card, 2) In the consent section, it might help to add a short note that staff should give a simple verbal explanation before asking for signature, especially for older adults. On responsibilities, the handoff to the nurse is clear, but maybe we should specify who is responsible for checking that the consent form is signed when a carer signs on behalf of the patient.

Good points. For carers signing, I suggest we assign the first check to admin staff at the desk and a second confirmation to the nurse before any clinical intervention. We can add that to the responsibilities table in A2 under T2. That way, both admin and clinical staff know their part and we reduce the risk of missing or unclear consent.

On the forms in A3, I noticed that the adult and older adult templates are almost the same. In practice, for older adults we often need extra contact details for family or carers. Could we add a dedicated section for emergency contact and main carer contact on the older adult form. Also, the disability support form has a free text box for disability details. I wonder if we should add a few guiding options, like mobility, communication, or cognitive support, to make it easier to fill in.

From the disability clinic side, having some guiding options on the form would help a lot. Many carers ask what to write. Maybe we can keep the free text but add checkboxes for the main support areas. I am not sure if that has any impact on data protection, so we might need the quality and compliance officer to confirm.

I checked the consent section in A3. The wording looks clear, but I wonder if we should add a short line that patients can withdraw consent later, as long as it follows our policy. I have seen this in other forms and it reassures people. I do not feel confident deciding this alone, so we should ask the quality and compliance officer to review that part carefully.

Thanks for the detailed feedback. I will update A2 to: 1) clarify ID checks against both appointment list and health card, 2) add a step for simple verbal explanation of consent before signature, 3) assign primary consent completeness check to admin and secondary confirmation to the nurse, including when carers sign. For A3, I will add emergency and main carer contact fields to the older adult form and propose checkboxes for key disability support areas, keeping a free text field. I will also add a draft line about the possibility to withdraw consent, clearly marked for review by the quality and compliance officer under T2 and T3.

Once you have the updated versions, I suggest we treat them as our candidate final set for the pilot and send them to the quality and compliance officer for formal review. Assuming they confirm that the consent wording and data fields are compliant, we can then lock the core SOP steps and the three form templates for adult, older adult, and disability support for use in the pilot.

Agree with that approach. From a practical point of view, the current draft of A2 with your planned edits covers registration, identification, consent, and basic information capture in a way that fits our daily work. The responsibilities table is clear enough for admin and nursing staff. I am comfortable using these steps in the pilot once compliance signs off.

For the forms, the three templates in A3 with the extra contact fields and disability checkboxes should work well in the general clinic and older adult unit. I do not see any missing fields for our usual cases. I support using these as the standard set for the pilot, again pending the quality and compliance officer review.

Same from the disability clinic side. The updated disability support form should reduce back and forth with carers. I am fine with using it in the pilot as long as we get confirmation that the extra details are acceptable from a data protection point of view.

One small suggestion: in A2, could we add a reminder near the end of the intake steps to store completed forms securely, in line with our confidentiality rules. It is something we do, but having it written might help new staff.

Good catch, I will add a step on secure storage of completed forms and alignment with data protection rules in A2. To summarise where we are: 1) We have a standard intake SOP that covers registration, identification, consent, and basic information capture with clear responsibilities for admin and clinical staff, 2) We have three unified intake and consent form templates for adult, older adult, and disability support cases, with the agreed adjustments. Next step is to send A2 and A3 to the quality and compliance officer for review under T2 and T3. If they approve without major changes, we will treat these as the final core steps and forms for the pilot.

threads.thread_goal: Lock training approach, materials, and schedule for the pilot

messages.text: Sharing the draft training deck and FAQ plus the healthcare assistant intake quick-check checklist for project_title: Rollout of Standardised Patient Intake and Admin Workflow. These correspond to A4 and A5 and are linked to T4, T5, and T6. Proposed training approach for the pilot unit: 1) two short live sessions per week over two weeks, 30 minutes each, 2) recording of one session plus the deck and FAQ shared for async review, 3) printed A4 quick-check for healthcare assistants at each station. Please comment on: a) whether the checklist is clear and fits on one page, b) if the mix of live and async works with shift patterns, c) any topics missing from the deck or FAQ.

Looking at A4, the checklist is clear and fits on one page. I like that it highlights ID check, consent explanation, and secure storage. One suggestion: can we add a small reminder to confirm if a carer is present and, if so, who signs the consent. On the training format, 30 minutes is realistic, but we should avoid the early morning rush. Late morning and mid-afternoon slots might work better for the older adult unit.

From the general clinic side, the mix of live and async in A5 works for me. Some colleagues prefer to read the FAQ quietly after their shift. For the live sessions, could we schedule at least one in the evening so late shift staff can join. On the checklist, maybe we can bold the step about checking that all mandatory fields on the form are filled before handing over to the nurse.

For the disability clinic, some staff are part-time and might not make the live sessions. The recording and FAQ in A5 will be important. Could we also include one or two short case examples in the deck, like a patient with a communication difficulty, to show how to handle consent and the disability form.

Agree on bolding the mandatory fields step in A4. That is where we often see issues. For the schedule under T5, I think we should coordinate with the head nurse to avoid overlap with medication rounds. I can help check typical times, but final confirmation should come from them.

On the training format, I support the proposal: short live sessions plus async materials. To make it concrete for T5 and T6, I suggest: 1) two live sessions in week one (late morning and late afternoon), 2) two in week two (one early afternoon, one early evening), 3) recording of the first session shared with all staff, 4) attendance tracked in a simple list. That should give most staff at least one option, and those who cannot attend can use the recording and FAQ.

I will update A4 to: 1) add a reminder to confirm if a carer is present and who signs consent, 2) bold the step about checking all mandatory fields before handover. For A5, I will add one or two short case examples for disability support and a slide on typical pitfalls we saw in A1. For the schedule, I will draft a calendar with the four sessions you suggested and share it with the clinic manager and head nurse for confirmation under T5.

The concrete schedule you proposed looks workable. As long as we avoid early mornings and medication rounds, staff should be able to attend. I support using that as our target training format and schedule for the pilot unit.

I am also fine with that mix of live and async. The evening session in week two will help late shift staff. As long as the recording and FAQ in A5 are easy to find afterwards, I think this will cover most people.

The checklist changes sound good. For the disability clinic, I will make sure staff know where the printed A4 quick-check is kept. Maybe we can mention in A5 that each station should have a visible copy.
Agree with locking this training approach for the pilot. I will remind colleagues who cannot attend live to watch the recording and read the FAQ so we reach the attendance target under T6.

To summarise: 1) We will use the one-page A4 checklist with the agreed edits as the quick-reference for healthcare assistants, 2) Training format will be a mix of four 30-minute live sessions over two weeks plus recording, deck, and FAQ in A5 for async review, 3) We will propose specific late morning, afternoon, and early evening slots to the clinic manager and head nurse and adjust if they see conflicts. With that, we can treat the training format and materials as approved for the pilot, subject to minor tweaks from their feedback.

threads.thread_goal: Coordinate the pilot run and daily issue handling

messages.text: Pilot announcement for project_title: Rollout of Standardised Patient Intake and Admin Workflow. The clinic manager and head nurse have agreed that we run the pilot in the main general clinic unit. Proposed dates: start next Monday and run for two full weeks. During the pilot, we will use the new SOP and forms plus the quick-check checklist, and we will track errors, delays, and staff feedback in A6 under T7 and T8. This thread will be our place for daily async check-ins: please post short updates on how the new intake workflow is going, any issues, and any workarounds you are using.

Confirming with everyone: the pilot unit is the main general clinic, and the pilot window is next Monday through the Friday of the second week, so ten working days. I will note this under T7 as our official pilot period. Each day, please share: 1) any intake errors caught, 2) any noticeable delays at reception, 3) any feedback from nurses or healthcare assistants. I will consolidate this in A6.

Day 1 check-in: Morning was busy but the new forms worked fine. I had two cases where patients forgot to sign the consent, but the bold step on the checklist helped me catch it before handing over to the nurse. Waiting times were similar to usual. One nurse mentioned that the emergency contact field on the older adult form is helpful.

Day 1 late shift: We had one walk-in where the patient did not bring ID. The SOP in A2 says we should follow the existing exception process, which we did, but it slowed things down. Maybe we should add a small note in the checklist about what to do in that case so staff do not have to look it up. No critical incidents, just a bit of confusion.

I am supporting the general clinic two mornings this week. Today I noticed that carers appreciated the clearer disability section on the form. One carer asked if the information will be shared with other services. I followed our usual explanation, but maybe we should add a line in the FAQ to cover that question.

Day 2 early shift: No major issues. One small delay because a patient took longer to fill in the new form, but the nurse said the information was more complete than before. I logged this in A6 as a minor delay with positive feedback on data quality.

Thanks for flagging the no-ID case. For the rest of the pilot, please continue to follow the existing exception process, and I will note this as a candidate addition to the checklist and SOP for the post-pilot update under T9. For now, we should avoid changing the process mid-pilot unless there is a safety issue.

Good to hear that the checklist is helping catch missing signatures. Please keep noting these in A6 so we can compare error rates with the baseline. If you see any repeated confusion about specific fields, post here so we can decide whether to adjust the wording after the pilot.
Understood, we will stick to the current exception process for no-ID cases during the pilot. I will keep logging them in A6 with a short note so we can see how often it happens.

By Day 4, I have seen fewer missing signatures. Staff seem to be getting used to the new forms. One recurring question is where to note if the patient prefers phone or email contact. The form has both fields, but some colleagues are not sure which to prioritise.

For the rest of the pilot, please ask patients for their preferred contact method and tick that field, but still collect both if possible. I will add a note to A6 that this is a clarification we might want to build into the form instructions after the pilot under T9.
On Day 5, I had a carer ask again about data sharing. I gave the same explanation as before. No delays, but it confirms that adding a clear line in the FAQ would help. I logged the question in A6.

End of Week 1 summary from my shifts: 1) No critical incidents linked to the new workflow, 2) A few minor delays due to patients taking longer with the new forms, 3) Nurses report fewer missing emergency contacts. All logged in A6.

Thanks for the updates. From what we have so far in A6, the pilot is running without major issues. Please continue daily notes through the second week so we have enough data for the evaluation report. We will use this thread again at the end of Week 2 to confirm that the pilot ended as planned and that there were no critical incidents.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results and agree on adjustments and rollout plan

messages.text: I have shared the draft Pilot Evaluation and Recommendations Report for project_title: Rollout of Standardised Patient Intake and Admin Workflow, which is A7. It summarises the data from A6 and proposes adjustments to the SOP and forms in A2 and A3, plus a draft rollout plan under T9, T10, and T12. Key findings: 1) intake errors decreased compared to baseline, mainly fewer missing consent signatures and emergency contacts, 2) small initial delays that reduced by Week 2, 3) recurring questions about no-ID cases, preferred contact method, and data sharing with other services. Please review and comment on: a) the proposed changes to SOP and forms, b) the suggested rollout phases and monitoring routine.

On the SOP changes in A2, I support adding: 1) a clearer step for handling no-ID cases that references the existing exception process, 2) a note to ask for preferred contact method and record it, while still collecting both phone and email, 3) a reminder to give a simple explanation about data sharing and refer to the FAQ. These reflect what we saw in A6 and should reduce confusion. The change log in T9 looks complete to me.

For the forms in A3, the only adjustment I would add is a small note near the contact details explaining that we will use the preferred method first but may use the other if needed. That matches how we actually work. Otherwise, the forms performed well in the pilot. I agree with keeping the three templates as our standard set.

From the general clinic perspective, the proposed SOP and form changes in A2 and A3 match what we experienced. The no-ID clarification and the preferred contact note will help new staff. On the rollout plan in T10, I like the idea of phasing by unit, starting with the older adult unit and disability clinic next, then the remaining units.

For the disability clinic, the report in A7 reflects our feedback well. I agree with adding a clearer explanation in the FAQ and SOP about data sharing with other services. For the rollout, it might help if we schedule a short refresher session for disability staff when their unit goes live, even if they joined the pilot sessions.

On the monitoring routine in A8 and T12, the monthly checklist looks manageable. I like that it includes a quick review of errors, delays, and any new questions from staff. We just need to be clear who is responsible for filling it in for each unit.

For T12, the proposal is that each unit has a named contact, usually the management assistant or a delegate, who completes the monthly monitoring checklist and shares it with the clinic manager. I will add that explicitly to A8 and the implementation plan in T10. For the refresher sessions, we can include a short slot in the rollout plan for each unit, using the existing training materials in A5.

On the rollout phases in T10, I support the sequence in A7: 1) Phase 1: older adult unit and disability clinic, 2) Phase 2: remaining outpatient units, 3) Phase 3: review and decide whether to extend to any other relevant areas. Each phase would have a short local training, go-live date, and three months of monitoring using A8. Risks and mitigations listed in the plan look reasonable.

I agree with that rollout sequence. It follows the units that are closest to the pilot and should adapt more easily. As long as the clinic manager and head nurse validate the dates, I am comfortable moving ahead with this plan.

The change log in T9 is clear to me. It helps to see exactly what changed in A2 and A3 after the pilot. I do not have additional changes to suggest. I support treating these as the final versions once the quality and compliance officer confirms the updates.

For the disability clinic refresher, a 20-minute slot should be enough, mainly to walk through the disability form and the consent explanation. We can reuse the same slides from A5 and just focus on the parts that matter most to that unit.
I can take responsibility for the monthly monitoring checklist for the general clinic once we move to full rollout. It will help keep an eye on any new issues that appear over time.

Based on your feedback, I will finalise A2 and A3 with: 1) clarified no-ID handling, preferred contact method, and data sharing explanation in the SOP, 2) small wording tweaks on the forms about preferred contact and use of other methods if needed. I will update the change log in T9 and send the final documents plus the rollout plan in T10 and monitoring routine in T12 to the clinic manager, head nurse, and quality and compliance officer for validation.

From our side, I think we can say that the adjusted SOP and forms plus the rollout and monitoring plan are ready to be adopted, assuming leadership and compliance confirm. I recommend we treat the versions in A2, A3, A7, and A8 as our final proposal for full rollout.

Agree. The final proposal reflects what we learned in the pilot and gives a clear path for rollout and follow-up. Once leadership signs off, we can start preparing local communications and reminders for staff.

To close this thread: we have consensus on the adjusted SOP and forms in A2 and A3, the rollout implementation plan in T10, and the post-rollout monitoring routine in A8 and T12, as documented in A7. I will now package these for formal approval. In parallel, we can start drafting the communication pack under T11 so we are ready once the plan is validated.
